description: We are Sarawak Astronauts, a group of university students from Swinburne University of Technology Sarawak Campus. We are interested in creating solutions to solve real world problems. For this challenge, we are hoping to provide a friendly solution to the public to raise awareness of astronomy. Our team consists of hard-working, creative and intelligent young adults that strives to excel in this challenge.
summary:
StarXplorer is a web-based citizen science platform built around NASA’s SPHEREx mission. It tackles three problems: there is no easy way for the public to explore SPHEREx’s openly available infrared data, many people know and understand little about astronomy, and scientists are struggling to analyse a fast-growing volume of observations to find meaningful discoveries.

The platform turns raw SPHEREx data into an interactive experience through three features: Explore, Learn and Discover. Explore lets users view real SPHEREx images, track changes in the sky over time and study astronomical objects with tools such as image blinking, subtraction and stacking. Beginner and Expert modes make it suitable for both casual users and experienced astronomers. Learn offers interactive tutorials and training games that build users’ knowledge and prepare them to contribute to real science. Discover lets trained volunteers search uncatalogued regions of the sky, flag possible discoveries and submit candidates for scientific review. Automated checks and a reputation system help rank the most promising submissions.

Overall, StarXplorer connects scientific data with public engagement. It makes astronomy more accessible and invites people to take part in real research. It also lightens scientists’ workload by filtering out weaker candidates before experts review them manually.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

NASA's SPHEREx mission maps the whole sky in 102 infrared bands and revisits every part of it about every six months. All of this data is public, but there is no viewer designed for the general public, or for watching how the sky changes over time. Most people also know little about astronomy, so the raw data means little to them. Meanwhile, SPHEREx collects new data so quickly that scientists struggle to search through it all for significant discoveries.

StarXplorer is a web platform that turns SPHEREx data into something anyone can explore, learn from and contribute to. It is built around three parts: Explore, Learn and Discover.

 

Explore

Users pick one of five well-known targets, enter any sky coordinates, or jump to a random sky position. StarXplorer fetches the real SPHEREx images for that position and cleans them. It removes the zodiacal light, masks faulty pixels, aligns every exposure to the same north-up grid and uses one brightness scale across all dates. It then plays the snapshots as a time-lapse, so users can watch the sky change over time. Users can compare images in three ways:

- Blink: flip between snapshots taken on different dates.

- Difference: subtract one snapshot from another, so fixed stars cancel out and anything that moved or changed stands out.

- Stack: average the snapshots so faint, unmoving sources become visible.

Explore has two modes for two kinds of users:

- Beginner mode is for the public. It uses tips, false-colour images, a guided tour and plain-language explanations of each tool, so no professional knowledge is needed. On the five showcase targets, it also points users to the real science they can see in Expert mode.

- Expert mode is for scientists and advanced users. It shows measured brightness in greyscale and exact coordinates, and adds these tools:

- selection of any of the six detector arrays

- brightness-over-time charts (light curves) measured from the real images, for any position

- per-snapshot metadata, such as dates, exposure counts and contamination flags

- for the five showcase targets, results we measured from the real SPHEREx data:

- spectra across all six detector arrays (0.75–5 µm) for Epsilon Indi B and RW Aurigae, with water, methane and carbon monoxide absorption marked for Epsilon Indi B

- side-by-side images from all six arrays for Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae and WISE 0855

- measured motion compared with the catalogue value for Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B and WISE 0855

- Gaia DR3 catalogue overlays with one-year motion arrows, plus each target's predicted path from its catalogue motion

Every view can be shared through its URL. An SI assistant powered by Google Gemini answers questions about whatever the user is looking at.

 

Learn

Interactive tutorials and training games teach users how to spot moving and changing objects, how to use the comparison tools and how to tell real objects from glitches such as cosmic-ray hits. These lessons give the public the foundation they need before they start making real discoveries.

 

Discover

Discover is where trained volunteers search new patches of sky (typed in or random, beyond the known showcase targets) and flag possible discoveries. Each submission goes through automatic checks:

- If no clear source appears in both snapshots, or the source has not moved, it is marked a likely artefact.

- If it passes the checks, it goes into a review queue for scientists.

In a full version, finds that match a known catalogue object, such as a Gaia star or a known asteroid, would also be marked "already known". This prototype does not yet query those catalogues.

Scientists use their own Submissions dashboard to review candidates and give a verdict. Useful finds earn points and raise the volunteer's reputation. Rejected or failed submissions lower it. Reputation sets each volunteer's priority in the review queue and how long they must wait between submissions. As a result, scientists see the most promising candidates first and are not flooded with low-quality ones.

                                                                                                                  

What benefits does it have?

- Gives the public an easy way to explore real NASA SPHEREx data, with no astronomy software or prior knowledge needed.

- Raises public awareness of astronomy by showing people how to spot changes in the sky and how to analyse them.

- Adds more volunteers to the search for discoveries, which reduces scientists' workload.

- The automatic checks and reputation-based ranking filter and order submissions before a scientist reviews them.

- Serves both beginners and experts on one platform, so neither group is left out.

What is the intended impact?

- Citizen science: let members of the public contribute to real scientific findings, as Zooniverse and Backyard Worlds do.

- Inspiring the next generation: nurture a passion for astronomy from childhood through games and hands-on exploration, so more young people consider careers in space science.

- Making use of open data: put SPHEREx's fast-growing public data to good use, so that more groundbreaking discoveries, such as nearby brown dwarfs, fast-moving stars or variable objects, can be found sooner.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did we use?

Languages

- JavaScript (React) for the frontend

- Python for the backend and science processing

Frontend

- React with Vite

- React Router for page navigation

- Tailwind CSS and Radix UI for the interface, with Lucide icons

- Zustand for app state

- HTML Canvas for the image viewer and the blink, difference and stack tools

- Recharts for light curves and spectra

- driver.js for the guided tour

Backend

- FastAPI and Uvicorn for the web API, with Pydantic for validation

- astropy for FITS images, coordinates and the wavelength of each image

- pyvo and astroquery for querying the astronomy archives

- reproject for aligning images onto a common grid

- NumPy and SciPy for image processing

- photutils for measuring brightness

- Pillow for producing images

Data sources

- NASA/IPAC IRSA archive: SPHEREx spectral images (data releases DR1 and QR3). We build the time-lapses from them and measure light curves, spectra and motion ourselves.

- ESA Gaia DR3 catalogue: star positions and motions for the overlays

- CDS SIMBAD: positions and catalogue motions of the five showcase targets

- 2MASS catalogue (through IRSA): used to check our brightness measurements, which agree with it to about 1 %

SI

- Google Gemini API (free tier) for the SI assistant, with a fallback model and offline answers if it is unavailable

- SI coding assistants (Claude Code, and Kiro running Claude) helped write, test and review code, under the team's direction

Hosting and development

- Render for hosting the website and the API

- GitHub for source control

- GitHub Actions for automated checks and a scheduled ping that keeps the API awake

Hardware

- No special hardware. It runs in any modern web browser on a computer or phone.

How is our project creative?

- Gamification: points, reputation and a ranked review queue make discovery feel like a game. The same system also improves the quality of what reaches scientists.

- Interactive tutorials and training games: users learn the real tools by using them, instead of reading manuals.

- Separate Beginner and Expert modes: one platform works for a curious student and a professional astronomer alike, without overwhelming one or limiting the other.

- Interactive time-lapse interface: watching the sky move with blink, difference and stack makes abstract infrared data easy to see and understand.

- LLM integration: an SI assistant explains, in plain words, whatever the user is currently looking at.

- A two-way loop between public and scientists: volunteers submit, scientists review, and the verdicts feed back into each volunteer's reputation.

What factors did our team consider?

Cost

- We used only free platforms and services: Render's free tier, the Gemini free tier, and the free public data archives of NASA, ESA and CDS.

Ease of use

- Accounts are hard-coded so judges can sign in as a volunteer or a scientist with one click, with no sign-up.

- Pre-computed real SPHEREx images for the five showcase targets keep the demo working even if NASA's servers are slow or down.

Catering to end users

- We designed for two groups: the public, who need simplicity and guidance, and scientists, who need full scientific controls and a manageable review queue.

Scalability, limitations and future work

- Accounts: accounts and submissions are currently stored in the user's browser, so a scientist only sees submissions made in the same browser. With more users, we would move to a proper shared database.

- Advanced tools for any position: spectra, six-array images, Gaia overlays and motion measurements are currently pre-computed for the five showcase targets. Computing them on demand for any position needs about 100 image downloads per position, which a more powerful server could handle.

- Catalogue checks: Discover would check each submission against catalogues such as Gaia, CatWISE and known asteroids, so known objects are marked automatically.

- Data growth: as SPHEREx adds observations to its current data releases, the site picks them up automatically, and a new release (such as DR2) needs only one line of configuration. The time-lapses get longer and more features become possible.

- Hosting: a more powerful platform such as AWS would let us support more simultaneous users than Render's free tier.

- SI: with more budget, we could use more capable models than the free tier.

- Reliance on NASA's servers: live searches depend on NASA's public archive, so an outage there stops them (the five showcase targets keep working). We already cache recent downloads and retry failed requests, but the free host wipes the cache when it restarts. Persistent caching would keep recent views working during an outage.
